questions.title: Drag force on a falling sphere — SI base units & terminal velocity

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer:
FD is a force, so its base units are kg m s⁻².
ρ has units kg m⁻³, A has units m² and v has units m s⁻¹ (so v² has units m² s⁻²).
Substituting: kg m s⁻² = C × (kg m⁻³)(m²)(m² s⁻²) = C × kg m s⁻²
All unit terms cancel, so C has no units (it is dimensionless).

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer:
Draw and label two arrows acting through the centre of the sphere:
Weight W — vertically downward.
Drag force FD (air resistance / viscous force) — vertically upward.
Both arrows vertical (within 10° of the vertical); at terminal velocity the two forces are equal in magnitude.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
At terminal velocity the sphere is in equilibrium (no resultant force), so the drag force equals the weight:
FD = mg = 0.049 × 9.81 = 0.48 N

questions.title: Ball thrown over a wall — projectile time, velocity & height

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement (change in displacement per unit time, in a stated direction).

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
Horizontal component of velocity = 22 cos 40° = 16.9 m s⁻¹; this remains constant during the flight (air resistance negligible).
t = 36/16.9 = 2.1 s

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer:
s = ut + ½at², with u = 14 m s⁻¹, a = −9.81 m s⁻² and t = 2.1 s:
s = (14 × 2.1) + (½ × −9.81 × 2.1²) = 29.4 − 21.6 = 7.8 m (rise above the release point)
height of wall h = 7.8 + 1.2 = 9.0 m

questions.title: Two-dimensional collision and braking — momentum & work done

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after the collision, provided no (resultant) external force acts on the system (i.e. for an isolated system). Momentum is conserved.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer:
Along the original direction of motion:
2m × 5.0 = 2mv cos 30° + 3mw cos 30°
Perpendicular to the motion:
2mv sin 30° = 3mw sin 30° → v = 1.5w
Substituting: 10m = 2m(1.5w)cos 30° + 3mw cos 30° = 6mw cos 30°
w = 10/(6 cos 30°) = 10/5.196 = 1.9 m s⁻¹
v = 1.5 × 1.9 = 2.9 m s⁻¹

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
Work done by the braking force = kinetic energy lost:
Ek = ½mv² = ½ × 4.2 × 6.0² = 76 J
F = W/d = 76/0.050 = 1500 N

questions.title: Copper wire — Young modulus, stress-strain graph & comparison

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Strain is the extension per unit original length (extension/original length).

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
stress = F/A = 18/(4.5×10⁻⁷) = 4.0×10⁷ Pa
strain = e/L = 1.4×10⁻³/4.0 = 3.5×10⁻⁴
Young modulus = stress/strain = 4.0×10⁷/(3.5×10⁻⁴) = 1.1×10¹¹ Pa

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: Draw a straight line through the origin (up to the limit of proportionality, stress is proportional to strain), ending at the point (3.5 × 10⁻⁴, 4.0 × 10⁷ Pa) — the top-right of the plotted grid.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
The second wire has a larger diameter, so a larger cross-sectional area A.
Same force: stress = F/A is less in the second wire.
Same material (same Young modulus): strain = stress/E is less in the second wire.

questions.title: Stationary wave on a stretched string — wavelength, phase & speed

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer:
The progressive wave travels along the string and is reflected at the fixed end (the wall / point Q).
The incident and reflected waves travel in opposite directions and superpose (interfere), forming a stationary wave with fixed nodes and antinodes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer:
From Fig. 5.2 the string (length 1.2 m) contains 1.5 complete wavelengths:
λ = 1.2/1.5 = 0.80 m

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
t = 0.24 s = 1.5T, so every point of the string is now at its maximum displacement on the opposite side of the equilibrium position.
Sketch the wave reflected in the horizontal dashed axis (inverted): the same wavelength and amplitude as at t = 0, crossing the axis at the same nodes.

parts.label: (d)
parts.answer:
A node lies between R and T (the points are on opposite sides of a node), so they oscillate in antiphase:
phase difference = 180°

questions.title: Cell with internal resistance — Kirchhoff's laws & terminal p.d.

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of the currents leaving it: ΣI(in) = ΣI(out) (the algebraic sum of the currents at a junction is zero).

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer:
By Kirchhoff's second law, the p.d. across the series combination is the sum of the individual p.d.s:
V = V1 + V2
Using V = IR: IRT = IR1 + IR2; dividing through by I gives RT = R1 + R2

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.answer:
Adding R3 in parallel with R2 decreases the total resistance of the circuit while the e.m.f. is unchanged.
The total current — and so the current in the cell — therefore increases.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.answer:
The larger current causes a larger p.d. across the internal resistance (Ir).
Since terminal p.d. V = E − Ir, the terminal p.d. of the cell decreases.

questions.title: Beta decay of copper-66 — spectrum, antineutrino & decay equation

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer:
Nucleon number = 29 + 37 = 66; proton number = 29.
⁶⁶₂₉Cu

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
The total energy released in each decay is fixed (constant), but Fig. 7.1 shows the β particles have a continuous range of kinetic energies up to a maximum value.
For energy (and momentum) to be conserved, another particle must be emitted to carry away the remaining energy — the difference between the total energy of the decay and the kinetic energy of the β particle.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: an (electron) antineutrino

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer:
⁶⁶₂₉Cu → ⁶⁶₃₀Zn + ⁰₋₁β + ⁰₀ν̄ₑ
Nucleon number is conserved: 66 = 66 + 0 + 0.
Charge is conserved: 29 = 30 + (−1) + 0.
